#8861. how sound, fungi, and material experimentation shape thomas feriero’s music project

composer thomas feriero discusses the three experimental systems behind 'will you still love me when i’m a system in the ground?', a collaboration that turns musical erosion, biological growth, and material transformation into a shared creative process.

‘Sometimes it’s only once the original sound starts to break down that you can hear something new taking shape,’ says Thomas Feriero, describing the thinking behind Will You Still Love Me When I’m A System In The Ground? The Milan-based composer, working under his new solo alias Challenging Conditions, has developed three experimental compositions that explore decay, distortion, and the unpredictable behavior of creative systems. In collaboration with Paris-based material design studio Aléa Work and designer Oscar Morgan, these sonic experiments extend into the physical world through a series of objects grown from mycelium.

The project brings together musical composition and biological growth, two processes that might initially appear unrelated. Yet, both involve interconnected elements that respond to one another, changing the structure and identity of the whole. ‘There is a shared language between sound and fungi – networks, waves, growth, decomposition and transformation,’ explain Miriam Josi and Stella Lee Prowse, co-founders of Aléa Work. ‘Both can appear chaotic while still generating new forms of order.’ For Feriero, the connection offered an opportunity to step outside familiar compositional routines. ‘The project began as a deliberate break with my own methods, because I wanted to step outside the routines I’d built over years of composing and see what would happen if I put both the music and myself in unfamiliar circumstances,’ he tells designboom. ‘Three experiments, or “systems,” came out of that, all developed in parallel and each a new way of making sound for me.’

What connects these experiments is an interest in things going slightly wrong. ‘I’ve always been drawn to those imperfections, but this time I wanted to give them more room,’ he explains. A friendship with someone developing a project about fungi and what grows out of decay had introduced Feriero to the subject years earlier. Although that original collaboration never materialized, the idea stayed with him. When Morgan later heard his musical experiments and connected them to Aléa Work’s research into mycelium, the relationship between the two practices began to take shape.

The structure of the project was shaped through conversation. Initially, Feriero considered the three musical experiments independent works, each governed by its own rules. ‘I didn’t design the structure in advance, and until Oscar heard the material, I’d treated each experiment as self-contained, with its own rules and logic,’ he shares with us. Morgan’s observation that Feriero seemed to be making music as difficult as possible to create became a turning point. ‘Each Condition is a set of obstacles I built for myself, both a method and a problem to solve, and the name also describes what the music is subjected to,’ Thomas Feriero explains. ‘To be completely honest, I was more interested in the process than the destination, and I think it was exploratory from beginning to end for everyone involved.’ The three Conditions each investigate a different form of sonic erosion: behavioral, physical, and structural. Their accompanying mycelium objects follow the same logic, translating the processes of the recordings into experiments with the material.

The first, Condition 01, uses physical modeling to simulate a jazz ensemble. Feriero builds digital instruments by simulating the physical behavior of their components, such as a vibrating string or the air moving inside a tube. Each instrument continuously adjusts to the others, producing a performance in which the sounds shift away from their original identities. ‘Every parameter is in motion and each player adjusts to the others, so a saxophone might slowly become a double bass before collapsing into something like a kick drum,’ he notes. The composition develops through these exchanges, with the ensemble gradually losing its cohesion while generating unexpected musical relationships.

Its material counterpart is a series of glass Petri dishes containing Pleurotus ostreatus, commonly known as oyster mushroom, mycelium grown on cotton fabric. During a two-week period in Paris, the dishes were placed in a room where the composition played continuously, allowing sound to become part of the growing environment. ‘For Condition 01 we wanted the music and the mycelium to actually share a space, so we rented a room in Paris where the piece played continuously while the mycelium grew,’ Feriero tells designboom. ‘The Petri dishes preserve that growth, now inert.’

Interestingly, the experiment did not influence the composition itself, which was already complete before the mycelium was introduced. What interested Feriero was the idea that the piece, already built around listening and interaction, could enter into a different kind of relationship with another living system. ‘The simulated players follow one another the way a pianist follows a bass player, and as they adjust to each other, the whole performance keeps shifting in a way that feels both broken and natural,’ the composer says. ‘I liked the idea of the mycelium as one more listener in the room, whose response, if it had one, would be in the way it grew.’ The Petri dishes preserve the physical outcome of a growing process that took place in its presence. The mycelium is dormant rather than dead and can be reactivated under the right conditions. The vinyl edition is limited to 100 copies, with 18 additional Bandcamp-only bundles pairing the record with an individual Petri dish.

Where the first Condition explores erosion through the behavior of simulated instruments, Condition 02 approaches it through physical degradation. ‘I took compositional sketches I’d discarded, recorded them onto cassette and put them through guitar pedals and increasingly absurd processing until all that was left was texture, a residue of the original music,’ Thomas Feriero explains.

Partly inspired by James Leyland Kirby’s work as The Caretaker, the recordings gradually lose their original structures, resulting in an extended collection of atmospheric drone, ambient passages, and percussive abstraction, in which the original compositions become difficult to recognize. The accompanying cassette is encased inside a composite mycelium brick that must be physically broken open to access the recording. Feriero sees this as an extension of the relationship between the recording and its physical presentation. ‘With Condition 02 it works the other way round, because the object has a say in how you get to the music,’ he describes. ‘We wanted the brick to feel like part of the piece, and for me that comes down to the choice you have to make when you’re holding one.’

‘There are only a few of them and no two are alike, so hearing the recording inside yours means breaking it open and giving up that particular object in its original form,’ the composer adds. The debris can subsequently be planted or used to display the cassette.

The final release, Condition 03, investigates erosion at a structural level. For this experiment, Feriero develops a small programming language to generate musical compositions entirely through rules before disrupting them. ‘In Condition 03 it’s structural, in that I wrote a small programming language to generate pieces entirely from rules, then quietly disrupted the pieces before the system could settle,’ he recalls. The digital composition is paired with a textile artwork exposed to mycelium growth.

Over time, the organism begins to strip away the color of the fabric and partially decompose its surface. As with the music, the process begins with an established framework but allows for outcomes that cannot be completely anticipated. Across the three Conditions, the material is never treated as fixed. Both sound and objects become records of processes that alter their original forms.

Feriero has worked across composition, sound design, installations, and software, often taking music into other contexts. ‘Most of my recent work involves making sound as part of something else, whether that’s a film, a space or a video game, and I think the collaborative side of that is part of what’s kept it interesting for me for over 20 years,’ he says. He points to an installation created for Milan Design Week, in which a choir was assembled from recordings of more than 65 friends’ voices. The work involved recording participants, developing the software, and deciding where the voices would play back, making the technical and collaborative framework as important as the composition itself.

‘I’ve spent a lot of time trying to make electronic sounds feel organic, so what was new for me here was thinking about what a piece could do once I’d finished writing it,’ the composer highlights. ‘What I like about the Petri dishes is that when you hold one, you’re holding something that grew in the presence of that music,’ he adds. The project also marks a new direction for Hidden Mountain, the Milan-based creative studio founded by Feriero, known for producing soundtracks for brands including Loewe, Louis Vuitton, Moncler, Nike, On, and Rimowa. Through Will You Still Love Me When I’m A System In The Ground?, the studio moves towards a more authored cultural program, using music releases, objects, and collaborations to explore alternative ways of presenting sound.

The conceptual framework and creative direction of the project come from Oscar Morgan, who developed the packaging concept with Feriero and Aléa Work, alongside packaging consultant Mino Kodama. Morgan’s initial interest in moving away from the digital landscape, combined with the references to mycelial networks in Robert Macfarlane’s Underland, helped establish a shared language for the collaboration.

#8860. Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

There are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on. But these symptoms, as vague as they are, could actually stem from a health condition that’s historically been deemed a “male disease”: obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA.

If you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone. It wasn’t until the ’90s that researchers first recognized that OSA, which causes you to repeatedly stop breathing while asleep, often presents differently in women than it does in men. For starters women with the condition may not even snore.

There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.

“The disease itself was defined in men,” explains Jennifer Martin, PhD, a behavioral sleep medicine specialist and professor at Florida International University’s Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine in Miami. “The way men and women breathe when they’re asleep is not the same, and our definition of the disease doesn’t account for that.”

Although obstructive sleep apnea appears to be less common and typically milder in women (at least before menopause), studies suggest that the consequences of the disease, if left untreated, can be similar, if not worse, for us, making it vital to learn the signs and seek help. Here’s what we know about obstructive sleep apnea and its impact on women. Plus, experts explain how to advocate for the best care if you think you may have the condition.

Sleep apnea is one of several conditions that fall under the sleep-disordered breathing umbrella. The most common type is OSA, which happens when your upper airway repeatedly collapses during sleep, making it harder for air to reach your lungs, says Anita Valanju Shelgikar, MD, a sleep medicine physician with University of Michigan Health and president of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

The textbook symptoms of this condition—which, for the record, were determined based on studies mostly involving men—include loud snoring and dramatic gasps for air as a person tries to continue breathing while asleep. But this often isn’t the case for women, Dr. Shelgikar tells SELF. Instead, women with OSA are more likely to have nightmares, wake up multiple times a night, have trouble staying asleep, and deal with insomnia, which then causes symptoms like daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and mood swings. Women also have more hypopneas (shallow breaths with less oxygen flow), whereas men tend toward apneas (complete pauses in breathing).

Some experts speculate that it’s possible snoring isn’t commonly reported among women with this disorder because they’re embarrassed to talk about it, given society expects them to sleep like Disney princesses. But a growing body of research suggests that biology may better explain this and other sex-related differences in symptoms. For example, compared with men, women have smaller, more stable airways that are less likely to collapse (and in turn vibrate, making you snore) during sleep. Women also tend to have less fat around their necks, and before menopause they seemingly benefit from the protective effects of estrogen and progesterone, which interact with the respiratory system in a way that aids breathing.

All things considered, it makes sense why more men than women in the US have this condition, making up about 59% and 41% of obstructive sleep apnea patients, respectively. However, once women go through menopause, which causes their estrogen and progesterone levels to drop, the rate of OSA and the severity of symptoms in this group increases dramatically, Dr. Martin says. Studies have found that anywhere from 47% to 67% of postmenopausal women have obstructive sleep apnea, which is about the same as men in this age range (50 and older). The number of women who actually get diagnosed with the condition is a different story, though—more on that shortly.

Regardless of age, however, women still deal with more sleep apnea–related symptoms than men, Dr. Martin adds, even if they have a less severe form of the condition. This is likely because women have more “subtle breathing disturbances” during sleep that hurt the overall quality of their rest compared with men, Dr. Martin says.

Because women often don’t experience “classic” OSA symptoms, they end up being misdiagnosed or dismissed. “When [men] walk into a physician’s office and say they’re sleepy and they snore, they get a diagnostic test right away,” Dr. Martin says. “When a woman walks in and says, ‘I don’t sleep well, and I’m very fatigued during the day,’ they don’t often get referred” for screening. In fact, research suggests that men are nine times more likely to be referred for diagnostic testing than women.

Women with OSA commonly have their symptoms misattributed to conditions like depression, anxiety, insomnia, and menopause or even medication side effects, says Dr. Shelgikar, who is also a neurology professor at the University of Michigan Medical School. Not to mention women can have these other conditions as well, which might make their sleep apnea not only harder to detect but also worsen it. Take the double whammy that is insomnia and OSA: Having both of these disorders at the same time is more common among women than men, Dr. Martin says, and in some cases they may be given a sleep aid (such as diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine) that can further relax their throat muscles, exacerbating their sleep apnea and leaving them even more oxygen-deprived.

And it doesn’t help that, as we talked about earlier, the diagnostic criteria for OSA are largely based on how the condition presents in men. “When we diagnose sleep apnea, we require one of two things to happen: A breathing interruption has to be associated either with a drop in oxygen levels or a brief awakening from sleep,” Dr. Martin says. “Women don’t have those very deep drops in oxygen levels that men do. So that means that the way we define the disease itself kind of biases us towards diagnosing it more in men than women.” What’s more, Medicare, which the vast majority of Americans ages 65 and older rely on for health insurance, only recognizes a sleep apnea diagnosis if a person has those steep drops in oxygen, Dr. Martin says. Those typical mid-slumber wake-ups don’t count on their own. So even “the criteria that Medicare forces people to use to define sleep apnea is very male-centric,” she adds.

Home sleep apnea tests, which are becoming increasingly common as a cheaper alternative to the gold standard in-lab exams, are also more prone to miss the condition in women. Because women tend to have fewer and milder events than men, these at-home tests may not be able to diagnose sleep apnea as accurately in this population, Dr. Martin says. They can be even more inaccurate in women with insomnia. These individuals “may not get enough sleep to get an accurate diagnosis,” she says, “so if they wear [the monitor] for six hours, but they’re only sleeping for four of them, it may look like they have less sleep apnea than they really do.”

That’s all to say that sleep apnea is likely much more common among women than the available data suggests, experts tell SELF. And that reality reveals a sobering point: A lot of women with this condition probably aren’t receiving the care they need, a delay that can, for some people, snowball into an avalanche of additional yet preventable health issues.

If left untreated, sleep apnea can have downstream effects on your health, particularly your heart, says Atul Malhotra, MD, research chief of pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine at UC San Diego Health. Every time you stop breathing, your body responds to the lack of oxygen by releasing the stress hormone adrenaline to jolt you awake so you take a breath. This happens really quickly; you are typically up for just a few seconds and probably won’t even remember it the next morning.

Over time this constant stress strains your cardiovascular system, Dr. Malhotra says, which may increase your risk for high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, irregular heartbeat, and heart failure. Although the evidence is mixed, some research suggests that it’s more common for women with severe sleep apnea to experience cardiovascular complications than it is for men. Studies also show that women tend to have more health conditions upon diagnosis than men do, including thyroid disease, asthma, and depression. This raises the classic “chicken or the egg” question, but either way treating OSA can only help.

Because obstructive sleep apnea leads to low-quality shut-eye, it is also associated with memory and cognition issues and poor daytime alertness, which can boost the likelihood of car and workplace accidents (for certain high-risk jobs like those in the transportation and construction industries), Dr. Shelgikar says. Perhaps less discussed is how untreated sleep apnea affects our ability to care for ourselves and maintain relationships. “We don’t do a good job thinking about sleep apnea as a potential cause of mental health symptoms,” Dr. Martin says. In fact, research shows that managing OSA could actually help some people dealing with anxiety and depression improve their symptoms.

As researchers continue searching for answers, Dr. Martin points to a silver lining: There’s good evidence to suggest that women “benefit at least as much as men, if not more” from sleep apnea treatment, which is why it’s important to know what to look out for.

Although you’re quite literally working against decades of medical bias, it’s still possible to receive a sleep apnea diagnosis if you’re equipped with the right intel.

#8858. RSHP centres cantilevered office building Sąvaržėlė around glass atrium

UK studio RSHP has revealed its first project in the Baltic region, a mixed-use office building in Lithuania designed as “a landmark that is unmistakably forward-looking”.

Named after the Lithuanian word for paperclip, the seven-storey Sąvaržėlė is located in central Vilnius, between the UNESCO-listed Old Town and the city’s commercial district.

The stacked building has a cantilevered design and houses office space, a conference hall, a restaurant and a cafe across its 19,000-square-metre space.

“At Sąvaržėlė, we wanted to create a workplace that extends into the city – one that welcomes people, encourages collaboration and contributes new public spaces to Vilnius,” RSHP associate director Jack Evans-Newton said.

“Occupying a unique position between the historic centre and the city’s emerging business district, the building brings these two identities together through a calm and contemporary architectural expression,” he continued.

“Clarity of form, generous public spaces and carefully crafted detailing create a landmark that is unmistakably forward-looking, reflecting the ambition of a growing business district while respecting the scale and character of its historic setting.”

Sąvaržėlė has large, adaptable floorplates, designed to create a flexible interior.

The building has a stacked, rectangular shape and was made from prefabricated steel components that were bolted together on site. On the east and west facades, RSHP placed external ribs that the studio said “echo the tones” of Vilnius’ historic architecture.

Sąvaržėlė is arranged around a central glass atrium with a striking yellow-lined elevator. It can be accessed via a number of different entrances that connect to the surrounding streets.

To enhance the building’s environmental performance, RSHP added a double-skin facade. This uses energy-efficient chilled beam cooling and automated natural ventilation to help reduce energy demand.

In addition, Sąvaržėlė has a 2,897-square-metre fully landscaped green roof.

RSHP has also recently designed a 45-storey skyscraper in Shenzhen and a curved-roof railway hub.

#8857. Bukhara Biennial 2027 Announces Theme and First Artists for an Edition of Lasting Public Works

The Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF) has announced The Long Welcome as the theme of the second Bukhara Biennial, which will run from September 3 to November 21, 2027, in the historic Silk Road city. The biennial, conceived and commissioned by Commissioner and ACDF Chairperson Gayane Umerova, is led this time by Artistic Director Kulapat Yantrasast, founder of WHY Architecture. It follows the inaugural edition, curated by Diana Campbell under the theme Recipes for Broken Hearts, which opened in September 2025. Bringing together Uzbek and international artists, the biennial will present new commissions made exclusively in Uzbekistan, and it aims to leave a lasting legacy in the city through permanent projects, from artist-designed gardens and fountains to installations in restored historic sites.

The biennial, conceived and commissioned by Commissioner and ACDF Chairperson Gayane Umerova, is led this time by Artistic Director Kulapat Yantrasast, founder of WHY Architecture. It follows the inaugural edition, curated by Diana Campbell under the theme Recipes for Broken Hearts, which opened in September 2025. Bringing together Uzbek and international artists, the biennial will present new commissions made exclusively in Uzbekistan, and it aims to leave a lasting legacy in the city through permanent projects, from artist-designed gardens and fountains to installations in restored historic sites.

For more than two thousand years, Bukhara has welcomed travelers who crossed deserts to reach it, a meeting point between East and West that grew rich on the exchange of goods, ideas, beliefs and techniques. The Long Welcome takes that history as its starting point and treats hospitality as a reciprocal act: an invitation for contemporary artists to encounter the city, learn from its people and contribute something enduring in return. Guided by the idea of culture as infrastructure, the commissions will range from temporary installations to permanent works, including gardens, fountains, benches and streetlights designed by artists, which will continue to serve residents long after the biennial closes.

The theme is shaped by four interconnected pillars. Local Hospitality draws on Bukhara's tradition of welcoming guests, with encounters with residents and their knowledge of the city informing what artists make, and some commissions becoming part of everyday life. Co-Creation builds on the 2025 model of pairing artists with local master craftspeople and extends it to collaborations with international institutions such as the Chanakya School of Craft in India, as well as new projects with ecologists, economists, historians, teachers, musicians and children. Resilience and Biodiversity brings ecological research into landscape-based commissions that address regional challenges, including water scarcity and air quality. Living Heritage supports the transmission of Bukhara's craft traditions, music and cultural knowledge across generations, and includes the return of restored madrasas and mosques to public use.

#8856. Can Swapping Out Your Plasma Slow the Aging Process?

Discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended). One of the latest clock-reversing experiments causing a buzz is a technique called therapeutic plasma exchange, a procedure that filters and replaces the liquid portion of your blood. A 2025 study in Aging Cell suggests the technique could lower biological age by two and a half years.

But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s important to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about new plasma as an anti-aging elixir.

Plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream. Although it’s mostly water, it’s also rich in proteins, metabolites, hormones, and inflammatory signals—molecules that reflect and influence what’s happening across your organ systems, Andrea Maier, MD, PhD, geriatrician and board member of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research, tells SELF.

“It’s a transport system like DHL, a vehicle to bring things from your brain to your muscles, from kidney to lungs, and so on. So it’s fluid with lots of information,” she says.

This makes it a smart focal point for longevity studies because it can capture a wide-angle view of your body’s internal state, also sometimes called your “biological age.” By measuring changes in the levels of thousands of circulating proteins in your plasma, you can get some sense of how well you’re functioning.

What that means is you may be 40, but your biology acts more like that of a 30-year-old—or a 50-year-old. It’s not a fixed or precise measurement, but it’s helpful health information, Keenan Walker, PhD, senior investigator at the National Institute on Aging, tells SELF.

“There’s no one biological age, but people try to estimate it,” he says. “And what studies have found is that people whose biological age is older than their chronological age are at greater risk for chronic conditions, diseases, and mortality.”

About 15 years ago, researchers started exploring the connection between plasma and the aging process. This led to experiments using a process called parabiosis, a surgical technique that links together the circulatory systems of two different organisms. In studies, researchers would stitch together the systems of old mice and young mice, with the hypothesis that if you circulated younger plasma in an older organism, the older organism’s body would reap the benefits.

And the studies did show that. Older mice who received the plasma of younger mice had more resilience to tissue and organ stress. This led to the development of using plasma exchange as a way to treat certain autoimmune diseases, neurological disorders, and blood cancers.

“So everything really came out of that question: Is there something in our circulation we could get rid of or infuse into it to be able to live longer?” says Dr. Maier. But there’s not a definitive answer to that question—yet.

In the Aging Cell study, researchers enrolled 42 people and exchanged their plasma with purified albumin (a blood protein) and saline. Some participants also got a type of immune therapy called IVIG added in. Researchers measured changes in their bodies with advanced lab tests that track aging at the molecular level.

At first glance, the results look significant: Some people in the study reduced their biological age by roughly 2.5 years. But Dr. Maier points out that this data comes from the middle of the study, not the end.

“If you are digging a little bit deeper, this ‘2.5 years younger’ is comparing people at midterm to the baseline, not at the end of the study and the baseline. At the end, the effect was nearly gone,” she says.

Part of the reason for this, says Dr. Maier, is you overwhelm your body when you take all its plasma out and reintroduce different plasma. The influx of young cells can produce a shift in your biological age, but then your body starts experiencing stress as it adapts to this major change, and your biomarkers swing back to what they were before. In other words, you may get some rejuvenation in the short-term, but it’s temporary.

Another noteworthy detail about the study was the health of the participants, says Dr. Walker. “Those who were less healthy saw a stronger intervention effect,” he says. “So I think it'll be important to find out for whom this works.”

As a concept, both Drs. Maier and Walker see some promise in blood-based interventions for improving overall health but hope to see a more personalized approach rather than a generalized non-specific plasma filtering process.

“I would call this a phase 1 study,” says Dr. Maier. “We’ve basically learned that we can safely do it, and now we have to see it in much bigger studies and look at the long-term effect. It’s not a crazy idea. It’s absolutely grounded in lots of evidence, but not for everybody. It needs to be more precise. The future is great in our field, and this is the first tiny step, but we should absolutely not implement it now in clinical practice because it is so rough on the body. I love innovation, and I love this study, but I think the future will give something else.”

#8855. podcast: how to create utopia for everyone when architecture scales to the metropolis

from resident-voted skyscrapers in mumbai to adaptive structural grids, the final episode of the room for utopias podcast series explores what happens when ideals scale up.

Because one person’s utopia rarely matches another’s, architecture only succeeds at a civic scale when it stops being a solitary monument and becomes a collective negotiation. Closing the Room for Utopias podcast series produced in collaboration with INDX|GLOBAL during Paris Design Week 2026, the final episode explores how personal design visions transform into shared urban realities. Hosted by designboom’s Managing Editor, Iñaki Laguardia, the conversation brings together two senior Indian architects — Carl Bhesania of Talati & Partners and Karl Wadia of Architect Hafeez Contractor — under the theme Can Utopia Scale?, examining how resident-led redevelopment and multi-generational practices allow an idea to belong to the many rather than the few.

During the conversation, the discussion turns toward Mumbai to test what happens when utopian ambition meets the realities of a dense, rapidly evolving metropolis. In India’s financial capital, acute land scarcity has catalyzed a sweeping wave of site redevelopment that is reshaping the urban fabric from the ground up. Existing housing plots are systematically replaced with higher-density structures, expanding residential capacity while restoring commercial affordability across the city. Within this transformation, a distinct civic mechanism has emerged: resident housing societies evaluate competing proposals from developers and architects, voting directly on the future form of their own neighborhoods.

‘Mumbai is the first city on the planet where for every single new development, the decision on how it looks, the decision on how that building sits on its site, is actually being democratically selected by the people who live there in advance,’ Wadia observes.

This resident-driven momentum has sparked a contemporary revival of Mumbai’s historic Art Deco vernacular — an architectural language inherently suited to the region’s intense sunlight and monsoon rains through deep overhangs and calibrated window-to-wall ratios. Translating proportions originally conceived for low- and mid-rise coastal structures onto 200- to 250-meter towers presents a complex compositional challenge, requiring careful scaling of crowns, facades, and maintenance systems to preserve coherence at street level. Yet amid competing developers eager to make every tower a visual spectacle, urban harmony often depends on knowing when not to shout.

‘Sometimes the best architecture is the one that does its work quietly… the design should complement where the building is going to come up… We have to try and find that sweet spot between trying to do something new and at the same time not make it look alien,’ notes Carl Bhesania of Talati & Partners.

Reflecting on what contemporary practice must prioritize moving forward, both speakers reject the archetype of the isolated auteur in favor of collective intelligence and long-term adaptability. Karl Wadia of Architect Hafeez Contractor redefines architectural leadership around openness across generational and disciplinary lines, emphasizing the value of listening: ‘when you have equal participation from men, women, from people with different abilities and disabilities, automatically it all starts falling into place.’ Bhesania echoes this call for humility, urging studios to build micro-level adaptive reuse into structural grids, such as column-free floor plates that accommodate shifting domestic and wellness routines over decades without demolition while embracing quiet architectural restraint over constant formal invention.

guests: Karl Wadia (Architect Hafeez Contractor | @architecthafeezcontractor) and Carl Bhesania (Talati & Partners | @talatiandpartners)

in partnership with: AMICI | @amici_india; MARMO SOLUTIONS | @marmosolutionsindia; AGGLOTECH | @agglotech

#8854. Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people. You might not immediately suspect a pulsing headache is due to allergies, but experts say it’s a common occurrence.

In fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb. That’s especially true “if you have multiple seasonal allergies, for instance to grass and tree pollen; live near farms; or spend a lot of time outside during allergy season, being bombarded by pollen,” says Beth Oller, MD, a family medicine physician in Stockton, Kansas. Keep reading to learn why allergies can spark headaches, plus how to tell if your head pain is allergy-related and find relief.

If you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr. Oller says, and releases a bunch of inflammatory chemicals like histamine. The resulting inflammation triggers swelling in your nasal cavities, which are connected to your sinuses, says Rekha Raveendran, MD, allergist and immunologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center. The sinuses extend behind the cheekbones, eyes, and bridge of the nose, and up into the forehead—so when they get puffy, you can wind up with a sensation of facial pressure and also headache, she explains.

At the same time, experiencing the effects of spring allergies may spark migraine attacks in those with migraine. The surge of inflammation and congestion can irritate a nearby nerve that plays a role in migraine, and allergy-driven fatigue and insomnia can be migraine triggers in and of themselves. Research suggests that among people with migraine, those who also have allergies tend to have worse, more frequent attacks than those who don’t.

An allergy headache typically feels like a dull throbbing in your temples, cheeks, or forehead, and makes your face feel heavy. It comes along with congestion, Dr. Oller says, and lying down or tilting your head can increase the pressure. (FYI: This is the same kind of pain as you’d get with a sinus headache, which is caused by a viral or bacterial infection in your sinuses—both lead to mucus buildup and swelling within the sinuses.)

By contrast, migraine attacks (whether or not they’re precipitated by allergies) trigger intense pain on one side of the head. They often come along with nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound, which you would not typically find with allergy headaches, Dr. Raveendran says. Meanwhile, tension headaches tend to feel more like a band squeezing around the head, and cluster headaches spark a surge of pain in or around one eye.

If you get walloped with allergy headaches each year, Dr. Oller suggests starting on an oral antihistamine medication before pollen counts rise. That's because antihistamines take a week or two of daily use to kick in, she explains. The non-drowsy options work best for daytime—think: cetirizine (Zyrtec), levocetirizine (Xyzal), loratadine (Claritin), or fexofenadine (Allegra). You can use the sleepiness-inducing diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at night, but just know that you shouldn’t make a habit of relying on it as a sleep aid.

Both doctors suggest pairing oral allergy meds with a nasal corticosteroid spray like fluticasone (Flonase) or triamcinolone (Nasocort). “They hit those mucus membranes and help decrease inflammation in that region,” Dr. Oller says. It’s best to take both drugs daily throughout allergy season, she adds, not just when you think you need them. (If your headaches are barely alleviated, or the pollen counts in your area are sky-high, you may also be able to safely increase your dose of these allergy meds to boost their efficacy.)

The less pollen that enters your airspace, the fewer symptoms you’ll experience. But you don’t have to stay cooped up to cut your exposure. Keeping your windows closed, using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter in your HVAC system (or a portable air purifier that has one), and vacuuming often can make a difference, according to Dr. Oller.

Whenever you do spend ample time outside, Dr. Oller says to rinse off once you get home. This way, you’re not inhaling pollen any longer than you have to. While you’re at it, “shower your sinuses too,” Dr. Oller adds, with a nasal saline spray or Neti Pot. This helps clear some mucus to release pressure and offer temporary relief, Dr. Raveendran says.

If the congestion is making it feel like your face is chock-full of mucus, you might be tempted to reach for an OTC oral decongestant. But take note: While pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) can be helpful, it’s not recommended to use it more than a few days in a row, and isn’t a good choice if you have high blood pressure, Dr. Raveendran says. It’s a stimulant that can make some people feel jittery, or cause a fast heart rate or insomnia.

Nasal decongestants, which include phenylephrine- or oxymetazoline-based sprays (like Afrin and Vicks Sinex), can open up your nose fast but should only be used for three days at a time max, Dr. Raveendran adds. “There’s a risk of rebound congestion that leads to overall worsening of symptoms and addiction to the nasal decongestants,” she says.

Sometimes you just need in-the-moment relief for the head pain. In that case, you can pop an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen (Advil), naproxen (Aleve), or acetaminophen (Tylenol), Dr. Oller says. The former two may be better at resolving allergy headaches because they combat inflammation. But it’s not advised to take these non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for more than 10 days straight (unless your doctor tells you otherwise) because of potential effects on your stomach and kidneys. Tylenol, by contrast, is generally safer to take long-term, though shouldn’t be combined with alcohol due to the risk for liver damage.

If you find that your allergy headaches have you reaching for pain relievers more than a few days in a row, check in with your primary care doctor or allergist. They may recommend a more intensive treatment, like prescription steroids, or suggest seeing an ear, nose, and throat doctor or neurologist, in case something else might be behind your head pain.

#8852. mara rethinks how we furnish modern, flexible office at orgatec 2026

mara unveils an ecosystem of flexible office furniture at orgatec 2026, which aims to shape the future of dynamic, remote-friendly workspaces.

The past decade has seen countless changes in the working landscape, and Mara’s furniture has evolved alongside them. Orgatec 2026, the trade fair dedicated to workplace design, provides the setting for the brand to present some of the latest developments helping to shape this world.

First came digitalization. Then lockdown. Finally, the rise of digital nomads. Offices around the world have witnessed continuous changes in workflows and in the understanding of work itself. Today, teams have flatter structures, remote work is commonplace, and everyday working life often takes shape through dynamic, fluid relationships.

Offices have necessarily changed in the process. From height-adjustable desks that prioritize health over the rigidity of the past to meeting rooms equipped with tailored furniture and buildings that integrate outdoor spaces into daily life, the environments we work in reflect the way we work. This is why Orgatec helps us take the pulse of how we furnish our offices and how we inhabit them.

Aligned with this increasingly fluid and flexible world, the collection Mara presents at Orgatec 2026 stands out for its versatility, flexibility, and durability.

One of the most talked-about developments is the expansion of its Aera collection. Designed by Marcello Ziliani, the seating system adapts to new needs with the addition of a writing tablet for the conference version, suitable for training, education, and meeting environments. The brand also introduces a new swivel version on a five-star base with casters, designed specifically for offices and collaborative spaces where mobility is essential.

Meanwhile, the Otto collection of height-adjustable tables, designed by Christophe Pillet, expands with new fixed-height versions.

Alongside these additions, Mara presents a new interpretation of a classic: Aera Metal, which draws on the brand’s metalworking roots. Retaining Aera’s lightweight, stackable, and practical character, the new all-metal version naturally extends into outdoor settings, helping create fluid spaces without boundaries. This proposal builds on Mara’s more than sixty years of metalworking experience and its commitment to durable, recyclable materials.

The Elle collection, designed by Ferruccio Laviani, also evolves. Specifically, Elle Boxes and Elle Wardrobe take it from a storage system to a multifunctional solution that structures a room as part of its architecture. It combines display, storage, and organization flexibly, responding to the needs of contemporary workplaces.

Orgatec also makes room for celebrations. Ten years have passed since Mara designed its iconic Argo Libro table system, created to meet an emerging need for flexibility in working environments. To mark the anniversary, the brand introduces a special limited edition in polished steel, transforming the piece into a mirrored surface that tells a story.

Beyond its own exhibition, Mara also participates in the Innovation Award Architecture+ Office 2026 installation with its Typo Lounge Chair & Ottoman, designed by AMDL CIRCLE, the studio founded by Michele De Lucchi. Additionally, the brand furnishes the shared seating areas in Hall 6.1 with its Aera chairs, Typo tables, Follow Break, and Typo Lounge Chair & Ottoman.

#8850. Lisbon Triennale Announces CO-OP and Herzog & de Meuron’s Memphis Museum Opens: This Week’s Review

This week's news explores how architecture responds to collective needs, environmental challenges, and changing cultural contexts. From the Lisbon Architecture Triennale's announcement of CO-OP as the theme for its 2028 edition to the recognition of Mexican practice COLECTIVO C733 with the inaugural Siza Award for Public Architecture, questions of cooperation and the public realm remain central. At COP31 in Antalya, discussions on building energy efficiency and urban resilience brought the built environment into focus, while the 2026 World Architecture Festival recognized projects engaging with environmental performance across different scales. Meanwhile, new cultural destinations are taking shape in Doha, Memphis, and Tulsa, where museum and pavilion projects reconsider the relationship between architecture, art, and public space.

This week's news explores how architecture responds to collective needs, environmental challenges, and changing cultural contexts. From the Lisbon Architecture Triennale's announcement of CO-OP as the theme for its 2028 edition to the recognition of Mexican practice COLECTIVO C733 with the inaugural Siza Award for Public Architecture, questions of cooperation and the public realm remain central. At COP31 in Antalya, discussions on building energy efficiency and urban resilience brought the built environment into focus, while the 2026 World Architecture Festival recognized projects engaging with environmental performance across different scales. Meanwhile, new cultural destinations are taking shape in Doha, Memphis, and Tulsa, where museum and pavilion projects reconsider the relationship between architecture, art, and public space.

Architecture, Cooperation, and the Public Realm

The relationship between architecture and collective life emerged through several announcements this week. The Lisbon Architecture Triennale selected CO-OP as the theme for its 2028 edition, with Chief Curator Joaquim Moreno proposing cooperation as a framework for examining housing, production, ownership, governance, and shared forms of living. The curatorial programme will explore how collective action shapes the production and use of space, extending the discussion from domestic arrangements to labour, landscape, and the common good. In Mexico, COLECTIVO C733 was named the inaugural recipient of the Siza Award for Public Architecture, established by the Serralves Foundation to recognize architectural generosity and engagement with public space. At COP31 in Antalya, the built environment featured in discussions on climate action through initiatives addressing energy efficiency, electrification, and urban resilience. The Turkish Presidency introduced the Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings, a voluntary framework targeting a 25% reduction in the operational energy intensity of the global building stock by 2035, compared with 2020 levels. Developed in collaboration with UNEP's Global Alliance for Buildings and Construction, the initiative outlines strategies for building renovation, reduced energy demand, efficient electrification, and improved building performance. Discussions also addressed how national climate commitments can translate into local investments in housing, infrastructure, and adaptation, while the Sustainable Urban Resilience Financing Facility (SURFF) was presented as a mechanism to connect cities with existing financing and technical support. Despite these sector-specific initiatives, disagreements over fossil fuels and climate finance prevented agreement on the proposed Antalya Pact, leaving broader questions about the international energy transition unresolved.

Questions of environmental performance and resource use also appeared among the projects recognized at the 2026 World Architecture Festival. The World Building of the Year award went to The Prestige University by Sanjay Puri Architects in Indore, India, whose stepped configuration draws on the spatial tradition of Indian stepwells while integrating courtyards that bring natural light into its interior spaces. The World Interior of the Year, &Matcha Three Yards by MLA at Home in the Philippines, uses open spaces, vegetation, water, and changing natural conditions to shape a small tea shop as a shared neighbourhood environment. Other winning projects approached environmental systems through different scales and disciplines, including Terreform ONE's Coding Kelp: Artificial Reef and Data Archive, named Future Project of the Year, and Natureza Urbana's Doca Linear Park in Brazil, awarded Landscape of the Year.

Qatar Museums Unveils Gerhard Richter's Permanent Doha Pavilion, Designed in Collaboration with Selldorf Architects

Qatar Museums has unveiled Doha Pavilion: Gerhard Richter, a permanent, site-specific structure conceived by the German artist in collaboration with Selldorf Architects. Located in MIA Park, outside the Museum of Islamic Art in Doha, the pavilion brings together a collection of Richter's paintings and sculptures, including a new work developed specifically for the space. Its hexagonal structure translates the artist's investigations into abstraction and perception into an architectural form, with six exterior walls featuring geometric patterns derived from his Patterns series. The design draws connections between Richter's mathematical approach to image-making and the repeating geometries of Islamic art. Realized as a legacy initiative of the Qatar-Germany 2017 Year of Culture, the pavilion joins other permanent public artworks in MIA Park and was unveiled as part of Qatar Creates Fall/Winter 2026–27, coinciding with the inaugural edition of Rubaiya Qatar.

Memphis Art Museum Opens New Herzog & de Meuron-Designed Building on the Mississippi River

The Memphis Art Museum will open its new building on the banks of the Mississippi River on December 6, 2026. Designed by Herzog & de Meuron, with archimania as architect of record, the project expands the museum's gallery space by 50 percent and increases its free public areas sixfold. Constructed primarily from laminated mass timber, the new building forms a two-acre urban campus with a 50,000-square-foot rooftop art park, a riverfront amphitheater, and a 10,000-square-foot community courtyard. Its inaugural program includes Making Beauty: Hooks Brothers Studio, 1907–1984, an exhibition of more than 150 photographs documenting Black life and culture in the urban South, alongside 15 presentations from the museum's collection and four site-specific commissions.

Tulsa's Gilcrease Museum to Reopen in March 2027 Following Six-Year Closure

After six years of closure, the Gilcrease Museum in Tulsa, Oklahoma, is set to reopen in March 2027 with a new purpose-built building. Designed by SmithGroup in consultation with the Osage Nation, the museum will house a collection of more than 300,000 objects spanning 12,000 years of art, history, and culture across the Americas. The collection includes Indigenous art and cultural materials, colonial Latin American works, American portraiture, and art of the American West. Located on a 460-acre campus overlooking the Osage Hills, the museum will also connect its galleries with the surrounding landscape through 14 miles of hiking and biking trails. Founded in 1949 by Thomas Gilcrease, a citizen of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation, the institution's reopening marks a new phase for its collection and research activities.

#8849. Meet BC Architects & Studies & Materials, Marina Tabassum's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler, two of BC Architects & Studies & Materials’ founders discuss how their ideas have gone from being perceived as the product of “young idealism” to being taken seriously by the construction sector.

The Brussels-based studio is at the forefront of bio-regional and circular design, with a whole arm of its practice dedicated to the development of new materials, often making use of construction waste.

Recently, the studio worked with UK studio Assemble and circular design lab Atelier Luma to create Le Magasin Électrique at Luma Arles in France, with a palette that included everything from rammed earth and construction waste to salt and algae.

Alongside these likeminded practitioners, BC Architects & Studies & Materials is at the forefront of a recent wave of interest in bio-based materials and vernacular methods – ideas that the studio has been championing for some 15 years, pushing for systemic change in the industry.

Founded between 2009 and 2012 by Ken De Cooman, Wes Degreef, Nicolas Coeckelberghs and Laurens Bekemans, the origins of BC Architects & Studies & Materials were – as its tripartite name suggests – not particularly conventional.

The studio is comprised of three different legal entities: BC Architects, an architecture cooperative; BC Studies, a non-profit “education laboratory”; and BC Materials, a material production co-operative.

BC Architects & Studies & Materials’s approach and outlook was borne out of a series of early projects in Burundi, Morocco and Ethiopia – where the studio briefly had a satellite office – which were grounded in working with local communities and materials.

“A lot of our first experiences in architecture were linked to different construction cultures,” said De Cooman. “I lived in Ethiopia for five years, others were in Morocco for a long time, and at the same time, we were finding our way in Belgium.”

“It was a different path to learning architecture as a practitioner,” he continued. We learnt to work with local materials and short supply chains, to make do with what you find around.”

The studio’s first built project was the Library of Muyinga in Burundi, developed using an open-source template from the OpenStructures network and constructed from compressed earth bricks alongside members of the local community.

It feels much more valid to be doing this in our own construction culture

BC Architects & Studies & Materials also designed several school buildings and a women’s shelter in Morocco, often using the construction process itself as an opportunity for the sharing of knowledge around vernacular construction techniques and materials.

According to De Cooman, however, this strand of the studio’s work was never intended to be long-term.

Challenging a tendency in the industry to view these methods and techniques as solely belonging to the realm of “humanitarian” architecture, BC Architects & Studies & Materials’s aim was to apply them to the business-as-usual processes of architecture and construction back home in Belgium.

“It feels much more valid to be doing this in our own construction culture,” said De Cooman.

“It was a huge learning process, and now we’re really focussing on the here and now because it’s here that we need to actually change the most.”

While a big part of this change is the studio’s use of alternative materials, it was also based on the idea of building being an opportunity for shared learning, driven by BC’s belief in the the need for architects to be more engaged with the construction process.

We’re still trying to emulate what our first experiences were: creating shared learning environments with people that can bring together different skills and learn from each other by really engaging with other field

Several of the studio’s early projects in Belgium the result of these learning workshops. Maison de Chasse, a rammed-earth hunting house, was constructed over the course of the first rammed earth workshop in Belgium, based on the techniques of Martin Rauch and Anna Heringer.

In 2017, the renovation of a series of warehouses in Ghent into an artist’s studio for Pascale Marthine Tayou was achieved via a five-week “Urban Construction Camp”, in which volunteers created a new hempcrete structure inside an existing metal shell.

“We’re still trying to emulate what our first experiences were: creating shared learning environments with people that can bring together different skills and learn from each other by really engaging with other fields, not on paper, but with the heart and the hands included,” explained De Cooman.

“It is crazy that we now have a system where, as an architect, you draw all the execution files and send them to a contractor to execute it exactly how you drew it.”

“The magic happens when everyone can get together – you can draw it together, find a passionate contractor to make it with.”

BC Architects & Studies & Materials was keen, however, to not be defined by this smaller-scale work, with the whole point being to demonstrate how these techniques and materials could be scaled up into larger contexts.

The idea of BC is to not only do small projects but also to change the building culture by making these materials available to big contractors and buildings

A key means to achieving this was the formal establishing of BC Materials in 2018, enabled by the interest generated by their earlier projects. Alongside consultancy, workshops and training, the BC Materials arm also offers its own range of earth and clay products, Léém.

“The idea of BC is to not only do small projects but also to change the building culture by making these materials available to big contractors and buildings,” says Wes Degreef.

“I think we were very surprised that the idea of working with a certain bioregion and its materials is something that we forgot in Europe.”

“Some of it still exists, but you really have to search for it. And with earth materials, for example, those crafts don’t exist anymore in Belgium. So we had to do it; we became the craftsmen.”

Sure enough, the scale of the projects involving BC Architects & Studies & Materials – whether they are engaged as architects or as craftspeople – is growing.

“In the beginning, we were just like young, crazy people who are doing these weird things on Belgium,” said De Cooman.

“There was a bit of interest in it, but it was also seen as, young, idealist energy. Now, we’re operating at a scale where we are actually seen as serious partners in the construction sector here in Belgium.”

There was a bit of interest in it, but it was also seen as, young, idealist energy. Now, we’re operating at a scale where we are actually seen as serious partners in the construction sector here in Belgium

In Brussels, BC Architects & Studies & Materials worked alongside EVR-architecten to convert a former barracks into the Usquare Feder university district, the materials for which were sourced in part by the dismantling of several neighbouring buildings.

With numerous other residential and office projects in the works – including a new bioregional materials hub and workspace in the centre of Brussels, Stadsatelierdeville, that will be its future office.

If it at times felt like BC Architects & Studies & Materials were up against the world, it is projects like La Magasin Électrique, which was a finalist for the 2026 Mies van Der Rohe Award, that reveal a growing international network who share their outlook, one that De Cooman is quick to credit with a lot of their own success.

“I think the dial is shifting, but I don’t think it is us who did it,” said De Cooman.

“There are all kinds of practises, organisations, material developers, and so on, who see a different construction sector – it’s a wave, a societal shift.”

“We’re very happy about it, but it’s broader than our practice. The construction sector is very conservative and we’re not there yet at all.”

Degreef adds that external social and economic pressures have also had a hand in forcing change to some degree.

“After Covid and the impacts on material prices, the gap between contemporary materials and the materials we want to promote is not so big anymore.”

Asked if there is a particular type of building that represents a dream project, however, they remain resolutely focused on processes and systems.

“I think, for us, it’s not in the buildings itself. It’s not what we build, but how we build and how everybody needs to build.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

#8848. hoor al qasimi appointed curator of the venice art biennale 2028

the sharjah art foundation founder will lead the 62nd international art exhibition, bringing her experience in cross-cultural exchange and international exhibition-making to venice

Hoor Al Qasimi has been appointed curator of the 62nd Venice Art Biennale, taking on the role of Director of the Visual Arts Department at La Biennale di Venezia ahead of the 2028 edition. The appointment places the Emirati curator in charge of the international exhibition, which opens to the public on April 8 and runs through November 26, 2028. Al Qasimi brings to Venice nearly two decades of experience directing the Sharjah Art Foundation, an institution she established in 2009 to support contemporary art and cultural exchange in the United Arab Emirates and internationally.

Her appointment comes with a curatorial practice shaped by an interest in different cultural geographies, historical narratives, and artistic perspectives. Since founding the Sharjah Art Foundation, Al Qasimi has developed an extensive program of exhibitions, commissions, and public initiatives, positioning Sharjah as an important meeting point for contemporary art. Among her recent projects is Sharjah Biennial 15 (2023), alongside the international touring retrospective of Hassan Sharif (2017–2018). She has also curated exhibitions dedicated to artists including Jorge Tacla, Leda Catunda, Bouchra Khalili, William Kentridge, Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian, Rasheed Araeen, Simone Fattal, and Yayoi Kusama.

Beyond Sharjah, Al Qasimi has held leading roles in several international art events. She curated the second Lahore Biennale in 2020 and served as artistic director of the sixth Aichi Triennale, A Time Between Ashes and Roses, in 2025. In 2026, she took on the artistic director role for the 25th Biennale of Sydney, titled Rememory. Her institutional responsibilities also extend across art, architecture, education, and cultural research. She serves as president of the International Biennial Association, the Sharjah Museums Authority, and the Africa Institute in Sharjah, among other positions. She is also the director of the Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

In announcing the appointment, La Biennale president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco highlighted Al Qasimi’s attention to cultural memory, the complexities of the present, and the relationships between places and their communities. He described her curatorial approach as one that brings different geographies and perspectives into dialogue, qualities he considers closely aligned with the institution’s international vocation. Al Qasimi, in turn, described the Venice exhibition as an important platform for artists and curators around the world. Recalling her first visit to the Biennale in 2003, shortly after beginning her curatorial work at the Sharjah Biennial, she said she was honored to take on the responsibility and looked forward to collaborating with the institution’s team.

The appointment establishes the curatorial direction for the 2028 edition, although its exhibition title, central theme, and participating artists have yet to be announced. Al Qasimi’s previous work offers some indication of the breadth of perspectives she may bring to Venice, particularly her sustained engagement with artistic practices and cultural histories that extend beyond established Western narratives.

event: 62nd International Art Exhibition, La Biennale di Venezia curator: Hoor Al Qasimi public opening: April 8 – November 26, 2028

#8847. Can You Actually ‘Boost’ Your Metabolism?

Few bodily processes are as focused on and as misunderstood as metabolism. It seems like just about everyone wants to “boost” or “speed up” their metabolism in the hopes of burning more calories and, as a result, losing body fat. In reality, this is not an easy task, but you wouldn’t know that from the countless TikToks claiming it’s as simple as taking a shot of apple cider vinegar, hopping into an infrared sauna, or braving a cold plunge.

The truth? Many of these supposed hacks don’t have much research backing them up, and the ones that do won’t meaningfully move the needle when it comes to your weight. Improving your metabolism actually boils down to a few basic tenets that aren’t flashy or sexy but can have long-term benefits for your overall health and well-being. We’ll get into all that, but first, a little background on what your metabolism even is.

Metabolism is commonly thought of as the mechanism that controls your weight. Having a “fast” metabolism means your body burns calories rapidly, making it easier to maintain or lose weight, while having a “slow” metabolism means you gain pounds more easily and have a harder time taking them off. This isn’t wrong, per se, but it doesn’t tell the whole story. Your metabolism is the way your body turns food into energy. This energy is then used to power your heart and lungs, build and repair tissue, regulate hormones, and perform other critical functions.

Put more succinctly, “metabolism is all the chemical processes that keep our body alive and functioning,” explains Jonathan Gabison, MD, an assistant professor of family medicine at the University of Michigan who is board-certified in obesity medicine.

For example, about 20% of the energy your metabolism provides goes to your brain, building neurotransmitters and keeping signals going, so having an efficient metabolism is critical for cognitive health.

In short, yes. Your metabolism is influenced by loads of factors, from genetics and age to weight. But that doesn’t mean your metabolism is fixed. It’s actually highly modifiable, says Shebani Sethi, MD, a clinical associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University and the founding director of the world’s first academic metabolic psychiatry clinical program.

That said, taking shots of apple cider vinegar in the morning or picking up “metabolism-boosting” supplements won’t do the trick. Research shows that improving your metabolism requires consistent long-term habits. Here are five that can make an impact.

Every time you move your body, it burns calories and raises your metabolism—both during the moment and for a period afterward. Think of your metabolism like a pie: Two thirds of the energy you use every day is devoted to keeping you alive (that’s your basal metabolic rate), and the rest goes toward digesting food and moving your body. Being more active is the most straightforward way to up your metabolism. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.

This can include dedicated exercise, like a jog, hike, or workout class. (The CDC recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.) But it also extends to all the movement you do outside of formal exercise, known as NEAT (non-exercise activity thermogenesis). Increasing your daily step count, prioritizing physical hobbies like gardening and walking your dog, or even taking on more household chores and grocery runs all count toward upping your overall movement.

Strength training helps build and maintain muscle mass. Muscle tissue is metabolically active, which means sustaining it burns more calories than maintaining fat tissue. Therefore, having more muscle mass will give your metabolism a slight boost.

By strength training you’re also improving your overall health. For instance, since muscle tissue uses the majority of the glucose in your bloodstream, more muscle mass can increase your body’s capacity to use glucose and help prevent blood sugar spikes. Plus, research has shown that having more muscle helps improve insulin sensitivity, including in individuals without diabetes.

Those same CDC exercise guidelines suggest including at least two days of strength training every week. That can include body-weight moves like push-ups and lunges; lifting weights with dumbbells, kettlebells, barbells, or cable machines; or utilizing resistance bands. Dr. Gabison says what’s most important is being consistent with your exercise routine, so it’s best to choose workouts you’re likely to stick with. And remember, if you’re just starting out, it’s important not to push yourself too hard early on and risk injury.

Protein is having a major moment right now. While things may be getting a little out of hand (hello, protein popcorn), consuming sufficient amounts of high-quality protein has well-established benefits for your metabolism. That’s because the nutrient is the building block of muscle, so eating enough of it helps support muscle growth and maintenance, especially if you’re resistance training.

Protein also has the highest thermic effect of all three macronutrients, meaning digesting it burns more calories than carbohydrates or fats. Plus, it’s the most satiating macro, so increasing your protein intake can help you feel fuller and fend off cravings, which may help with weight management.

However, balance is key. Sun Kim, MD, MS, a board-certified endocrinologist and associate professor of medicine at Stanford, says doctors and health care providers have different viewpoints on how much protein is enough for optimal health. In her opinion, “most Americans eat plenty of protein without trying,” she says, cautioning that consuming excessive amounts won’t magically speed up your metabolism and could even worsen insulin sensitivity in some cases. So unless you’re extremely active, there’s no need to get hundreds of grams a day.

For most healthy adults, the recommended dietary allowance for protein is 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day. That means a 120-pound person needs roughly 43 grams of protein a day, which is about what you’d find in two four-ounce hamburger patties. If you incorporate some protein into every snack and meal throughout the day, you should easily hit the mark. That said, some groups need more. People who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or highly active may need up to 2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. Older adults and those taking GLP-1s should also be mindful of their intake, as reduced appetite can lead to inadequate protein intake and muscle loss, particularly when coupled with reduced physical activity.

An often-overlooked habit for better metabolism is getting quality sleep. A lack of sleep dysregulates your metabolism, causing a cascade of issues, including worsened glucose management, more intense hunger the next day, and reduced energy expenditure. (Sleepy people are less likely to move their bodies.) When this happens consistently, it can lead to an increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Sleep also has an impact on hormones that can slow down the metabolism.

There isn’t a specific number of hours you should sleep each night, but research shows that most adults do best with seven to nine hours of quality rest most evenings.

Prolonged stress keeps your cortisol (stress hormone) levels chronically elevated, which can break down muscle tissue and slow your metabolism. Constantly pulling out your hair can also disrupt your appetite-regulating hormones, triggering cravings that may prompt you to eat more. All of these things can affect your weight. Research shows chronic stress can increase your risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and related cardiometabolic complications too.

There is, sadly, no quick fix for reducing stress, so some trial and error might be required to figure out what works best for you. Some places to start are doing yoga, meditating, practicing breathing exercises, going for walks outside, journaling, spending time with loved ones, engaging in relaxing hobbies, or starting therapy to talk through whatever is weighing on you.

Sure, supporting a healthy metabolism can increase the number of calories you burn and help with weight management. But it can also improve what’s known as your metabolic health, which encompasses measures such as blood pressure, cholesterol, insulin sensitivity, and total body fat. Having good metabolic health is essential for preventing chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes and heart disease. The healthier your metabolism, the more calories you burn and the better your metabolic health.

#8845. How to Plan and Visualize For a City That Has Yet to Be Built

While most cities develop gradually, building one from scratch is hardly a new concept. Starting with a blank site, however, brings its own set of challenges. Rather than responding to an existing urban fabric, planners must anticipate how an entire environment will function, from its streets and infrastructure to its public spaces and the relationships between them.

While most cities develop gradually, building one from scratch is hardly a new concept. Starting with a blank site, however, brings its own set of challenges. Rather than responding to an existing urban fabric, planners must anticipate how an entire environment will function, from its streets and infrastructure to its public spaces and the relationships between them.

Even with a masterplan in place, bringing that vision into reality requires continuous development and adjustment. This is where visualization becomes essential, with digital tools offering new ways to understand and communicate a city before it exists.

Even with a masterplan in place, bringing that vision into reality requires continuous development and adjustment. This is where visualization becomes essential, with digital tools offering new ways to understand and communicate a city before it exists.

Planning an entirely new city means considering several elements together:

Planning an entirely new city means considering several elements together:

Buildings and public spaces: How buildings relate to streets, squares, parks and surrounding neighborhoods; Movement and infrastructure: How roads, pedestrian routes and public transport connect different parts of the development; Landscape and surroundings: How green spaces, existing terrain and the wider environment fit into the plan; Changes over time: How visual material can be updated as building designs, infrastructure and other parts of the masterplan evolve.

Getting these relationships right helps people understand how a proposed development is intended to function as a place. It also means keeping visualizations aligned with the latest plans, without presenting undecided parts of the project as finished designs.

Bradfield City Center, a new 282-acre (114-hectare) development in Western Sydney brings these challenges into focus. Described as Australia's first major new city in more than a century, its masterplan includes buildings, streets, public spaces, landscaping and transport infrastructure.

Turning a large masterplan into a digital environment starts with building a detailed 3D model of the proposed site. Buildings, roads, terrain, vegetation and infrastructure need to be placed in relation to one another, with enough detail to support both aerial views and images from street level. As the design changes, the model and its materials also need to be updated, which can become time-consuming across a project of this scale.

A digital model of a proposed city can be presented in several ways, depending on what needs to be communicated and who needs to understand it:

A digital model of a proposed city can be presented in several ways, depending on what needs to be communicated and who needs to understand it:
